1. Run a citywide campaign explaining the difference between food safety dates and quality dates.
2. Offer free meal-planning workshops through libraries and community centers.
3. Teach residents how to store fruits and vegetables to extend their freshness.
4. Publish a seasonal recipe guide for using leftovers and commonly discarded ingredients.
5. Distribute refrigerator thermometers with guidance on safe storage temperatures.
6. Create a household food-waste tracking challenge with neighborhood prizes.
7. Offer cooking classes focused on making appropriately sized portions.
8. Provide multilingual food-storage and waste-prevention guides.
9. Encourage households to designate an “eat first” shelf in their refrigerators.
10. Organize community classes on safe freezing, canning, pickling, and drying.
11. Establish a citywide surplus-food matching platform connecting businesses with charities.
12. Fund refrigerated vans for food-rescue organizations.
13. Create neighborhood food-donation drop-off hubs with reliable refrigeration.
14. Offer small grants to help food pantries expand cold-storage capacity.
15. Recruit volunteer drivers to collect surplus food from local businesses.
16. Establish a rapid-response network for rescuing food after event cancellations.
17. Publish clear local guidance on food-donation safety requirements and liability protections.
18. Coordinate donation pickup schedules so businesses can participate consistently.
19. Create a food-rescue hotline for urgent, large-volume donations.
20. Support shared refrigerated storage for small charities awaiting deliveries.
21. Help grocery stores introduce dynamic discounts for products approaching their quality dates.
22. Encourage supermarkets to sell cosmetically imperfect produce at reduced prices.
23. Support grocery “rescue boxes” containing assorted surplus items.
24. Train grocery employees to rotate stock using first-expiring-first-out practices.
25. Help independent grocers adopt inventory systems that flag likely overstock.
26. Encourage stores to offer smaller package sizes without disproportionate price premiums.
27. Replace multibuy promotions on perishables with equivalent single-item discounts.
28. Encourage retailers to sell loose produce so shoppers can buy only what they need.
29. Help supermarkets revise appearance standards that cause edible produce to be rejected.
30. Recognize retailers that publicly report and reduce their food waste.
31. Provide restaurants with grants for food-waste measurement tools.
32. Train restaurant staff to distinguish avoidable waste from unavoidable preparation scraps.
33. Encourage restaurants to offer half portions and flexible side-dish sizes.
34. Make take-home containers routinely available for restaurant leftovers.
35. Encourage restaurants to ask before providing bread, chips, or other complimentary foods.
36. Help restaurants streamline menus to reduce seldom-used perishable ingredients.
37. Support restaurant forecasting tools that account for weather, reservations, and local events.
38. Create a surplus-meal marketplace for restaurants to sell unsold food before closing.
39. Encourage restaurants to use edible stems, leaves, and trimmings in suitable dishes.
40. Organize chef exchanges where kitchens share successful waste-reduction techniques.
41. Require food-waste prevention plans for large events receiving city permits.
42. Connect caterers with food-rescue partners before events take place.
43. Encourage event organizers to collect meal preferences and attendance confirmations in advance.
44. Promote smaller buffet serving trays that can be replenished as needed.
45. Offer caterers guidance on safely donating food that has not been served.
46. Provide event hosts with portion-planning calculators.
47. Establish reusable-container lending programs for community meals and festivals.
48. Encourage conference organizers to make leftover meals available to attendees when safe.
49. Include food-waste performance requirements in contracts for city-owned venues.
50. Offer lower permit fees to events that verify substantial food-waste prevention.
51. Help schools measure cafeteria waste through student-led audits.
52. Schedule school lunches after recess where practical so students arrive ready to eat.
53. Give students enough seated time to finish their meals.
54. Create supervised school share tables for eligible unopened or intact food.
55. Use student taste tests before adding new dishes to school menus.
56. Allow students to choose among nutritious meal components where regulations permit.
57. Teach food-waste prevention through school science, mathematics, and cooking lessons.
58. Establish safe donation channels for surplus school meals.
59. Use school meal participation data to improve purchasing and preparation forecasts.
60. Include food-waste prevention training in culinary and hospitality courses.
61. Organize gleaning teams to harvest produce left in nearby farm fields.
62. Create a fruit-tree harvesting network for residents with surplus backyard fruit.
63. Map publicly accessible edible trees and publish responsible harvesting guidance.
64. Help community gardens coordinate donations of surplus harvests.
65. Provide small farmers with shared cold-storage facilities near city markets.
66. Support mobile processing equipment that turns surplus produce into shelf-stable products.
67. Encourage farmers’ markets to arrange end-of-day surplus collection.
68. Develop markets for edible crops rejected because of size or shape.
69. Connect growers with institutional buyers for seasonal surpluses.
70. Offer microgrants for farm improvements that prevent harvest and storage losses.
71. Install community refrigerators with trained stewards and clear food-safety rules.
72. Create neighborhood food-sharing groups for unopened pantry items and garden surplus.
73. Establish food exchange shelves in apartment buildings where safe management is feasible.
74. Help housing providers create shared freezer space with clear labeling and maintenance rules.
75. Include food-storage guidance in welcome materials for new residents.
76. Partner with universities to collect unopened food when students move out.
77. Organize pantry cleanout drives before major holidays and school breaks.
78. Offer accessible cooking support for residents who struggle to use standard package sizes.
79. Coordinate culturally appropriate surplus-food distribution so recipients receive food they can use.
80. Let food-aid recipients choose items rather than receive fixed boxes whenever practical.
81. Conduct a citywide food-waste baseline study to identify the largest preventable losses.
82. Set measurable food-waste reduction targets for municipal operations.
83. Require city departments to track food purchased, served, donated, and discarded.
84. Update municipal purchasing contracts to allow flexible order quantities.
85. Train public-facility kitchen managers in demand forecasting and inventory control.
86. Create a cross-sector food-waste council with businesses, charities, residents, and researchers.
87. Publish an annual dashboard showing progress on prevention and edible-food recovery.
88. Offer competitive grants for locally tested food-waste prevention innovations.
89. Establish a business certification program based on verified food-waste reductions.
90. Integrate food-waste prevention advice into routine health-inspection outreach.
91. Help hospitals offer patient meal ordering closer to serving time.
92. Encourage senior-care facilities to tailor portions to residents’ appetites and preferences.
93. Equip workplace cafeterias to offer discounted surplus meals to employees.
94. Work with hotels to replace oversized breakfast buffets with smaller batches or made-to-order options.
95. Support bakeries in turning safe unsold bread into products such as breadcrumbs or croutons.
96. Connect food manufacturers with buyers for edible production byproducts.
97. Develop emergency plans to relocate perishable food during power outages.
98. Provide backup-power grants for food banks and other high-volume food-storage sites.
99. Divert food unsuitable for people to animal feed where legally permitted and nutritionally appropriate.
100. Provide separate collection and composting for unavoidable food scraps that cannot be safely eaten or otherwise recovered.

1. Launch a citywide campaign teaching residents how to plan meals around food they already have.
2. Offer free meal-planning workshops at libraries and community centers.
3. Distribute grocery-list templates that help shoppers avoid buying unnecessary perishables.
4. Teach residents the difference between food safety dates and quality dates.

9. Encourage households to designate an “eat first” shelf in their refrigerators.
10. Promote a weekly leftover night through neighborhood challenges.
11. Establish a lending library of food dehydrators, canning equipment, and vacuum sealers.
12. Hold safe home-preservation classes during peak harvest seasons.
13. Help residents learn appropriate portion sizes to reduce overcooking.
14. Recruit local chefs to demonstrate recipes using commonly discarded edible scraps.
15. Organize neighborhood swaps for unopened pantry items approaching their quality dates.
16. Install community refrigerators with clear food safety rules and reliable volunteer oversight.
17. Create small grants for neighborhood food-sharing projects.
18. Offer apartment buildings shared freezer space for safely storing surplus food.
19. Encourage residents to freeze surplus ingredients before they spoil.
20. Develop a move-out food donation program for renters and university students.
21. Require large food businesses to measure and report edible food waste.
22. Provide free food-waste audits for independent restaurants.
23. Help restaurants redesign menus so ingredients can be used across multiple dishes.
24. Train restaurant staff to use first-in, first-out inventory systems.
25. Offer grants for inventory software that helps food businesses prevent spoilage.
26. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portions at proportionately lower prices.
27. Make side dishes optional rather than automatically including them with every meal.
28. Encourage servers to ask customers before providing bread baskets.
29. Help restaurants replace oversized buffet trays with smaller batches replenished more often.
30. Promote preordering for catered events to improve meal-count estimates.
31. Create a restaurant surplus marketplace offering discounted meals near closing time.
32. Establish scheduled collection routes connecting restaurant surplus with food rescue organizations.
33. Provide businesses with standardized donation labels showing ingredients, allergens, and preparation times.
34. Offer food safety training specifically for businesses donating prepared meals.
35. Publicize applicable donor liability protections and their requirements.
36. Recognize restaurants that achieve verified reductions in food waste.
37. Encourage restaurants to offer take-home containers without customers having to request them.
38. Help commercial kitchens track plate waste separately from preparation waste.
39. Support commercial kitchens in safely using edible stems, peels, and trimmings in recipes.
40. Encourage reservation systems to send reminders that reduce no-shows and wasted meal preparation.
41. Help grocery stores introduce dynamic markdowns for products nearing their quality dates.
42. Encourage retailers to sell cosmetically imperfect produce at discounted prices.
43. Replace mandatory multipack promotions with discounts that also apply to single items.
44. Support grocery stores in improving demand forecasts using seasonal and sales data.
45. Encourage stores to use smaller produce displays that require less surplus inventory.
46. Help retailers improve refrigeration maintenance to prevent food losses.
47. Establish rapid donation alerts for grocery stores facing unexpected surplus.
48. Create a citywide system for rescuing safe food during store closures or refrigeration failures.
49. Encourage retailers to sell loose produce so customers can buy only what they need.
50. Support packaging trials that extend freshness without creating excessive packaging waste.
51. Help supermarkets turn suitable surplus ingredients into safely prepared deli products.
52. Encourage stores to stock smaller package sizes at fair unit prices.
53. Set up donation bins for suitable shelf-stable foods near grocery store exits.
54. Work with wholesalers to redirect rejected but safe shipments to local food assistance providers.
55. Create a shared cold-storage hub for food rescue groups.
56. Fund refrigerated vehicles for organizations transporting donated perishables.
57. Coordinate a single food rescue dispatch service to match donations with available recipients.
58. Extend food pantry hours so residents can collect perishable food after work.
59. Equip food pantries with freezers and refrigerators sized for their donation volumes.
60. Shift food pantries toward client-choice models to reduce unwanted food.
61. Survey food assistance recipients about dietary needs and preferred ingredients.
62. Provide recipes and preparation guidance alongside unfamiliar donated foods.
63. Develop emergency distribution plans for surplus food during storms and power outages.
64. Partner with transit agencies to improve access to food distribution sites.
65. Create paid food rescue coordinator positions rather than relying entirely on volunteers.
66. Conduct school cafeteria waste audits with student participation.
67. Schedule school recess before lunch where feasible to help students eat more of their meals.
68. Give students sufficient seated time to finish school meals.
69. Use student taste tests before adding dishes to school menus.
70. Establish supervised school share tables for eligible unopened foods under local safety rules.
71. Let students choose appropriate portion sizes when nutrition requirements permit.
72. Teach food storage, meal planning, and leftover cooking in school curricula.
73. Introduce school lunch preordering to reduce surplus preparation.
74. Donate eligible unserved school meals through approved recovery programs.
75. Install milk dispensers in suitable cafeterias to let students take amounts they will drink.
76. Require municipal catering contracts to include food-waste prevention plans.
77. Ask city departments to confirm attendance before ordering meeting refreshments.
78. Serve municipal event meals in stages rather than putting all food out at once.
79. Include surplus food donation arrangements in permits for major public events.
80. Offer reusable take-home containers at city-sponsored festivals.
81. Help hospitals forecast meal demand using patient counts and dietary requirements.
82. Encourage senior meal programs to offer portion choices suited to recipients’ appetites.
83. Require city-funded food programs to review purchasing against actual consumption.
84. Include food-waste prevention training in municipal workforce development programs.
85. Build a volunteer gleaning network to harvest surplus crops from nearby farms.
86. Organize seasonal harvest teams for fruit trees on public land and participating private properties.
87. Provide farmers’ markets with end-of-day donation collection services.
88. Help community gardens coordinate planting to avoid overwhelming seasonal gluts.
89. Create neighborhood crop-sharing boards for gardeners with excess produce.
90. Support local processors that turn surplus produce into frozen foods, sauces, or preserves.
91. Connect breweries, bakeries, and food manufacturers with businesses that can use their edible byproducts.
92. Develop approved animal-feed partnerships for suitable food residuals that cannot feed people.
93. Provide curbside collection of unavoidable food scraps for composting.
94. Require multifamily buildings to offer convenient food-scrap collection.
95. Install staffed food-scrap drop-off points at markets and community centers.
96. Support neighborhood composting sites with training, equipment, and pest-management assistance.
97. Send suitable non-edible food residuals to anaerobic digestion facilities that recover energy and nutrients.
98. Adopt waste collection pricing that rewards businesses for reducing discarded food without discouraging safe disposal.
99. Publish a city food-waste dashboard tracking prevention, donation, and organics recovery separately.
100. Set measurable citywide food-waste reduction targets and review progress annually with residents and businesses.
